title: Nkwobi
author: Chioma Adeleke
desc: Two kilos of cow foot in an emulsion of 200 ml palm oil and a tablespoon of potash — stirred until the oil curdles and turns yellow — served in a wooden mortar.
longDesc: Nkwobi is cow foot cooked until gelatinous and then dressed in the ncha emulsion. The technique is the emulsion and the cue is excellent: pour the sieved potash mixture into the palm oil in a clean dry pot, stirring with a wooden spatula as you pour, and you will notice the palm oil begin to curdle and turn yellow — keep stirring till all of it has. The clean dry pot is not a nicety; water breaks the emulsion. It arrives in a wooden mortar garnished with utazi slices and onion rings, and it is eaten with a cold drink.
ingredients: 2 kg (4.4 lbs) cow foot, cut into sizeable pieces
1 tbsp powdered edible potash (akanwu, kaun, keun)
equipment: Clean dry pot for the emulsion
steps: Clean and wash the cow foot thoroughly.
Boil with the stock cubes, the whole onion and salt until well done. Cow foot is slow — a pressure cooker saves a great deal of time.
Dissolve the potash in a small amount of water and sieve it, leaving the sediment behind.
Pour the palm oil into a clean dry pot.
Pour in the sieved potash mixture, stirring with a wooden spatula as you pour.
You'll notice the palm oil begin to curdle and turn yellow. Keep stirring till all the oil has turned yellow.
Add the ground ehu, the blended habanero and salt to the emulsion.
Fold in the cooked cow foot and mix until every piece is coated.
Heat gently until the nkwobi is piping hot.
Serve in a wooden mortar, garnished with thin utazi slices and onion rings.
chefTips: A clean dry pot. Water in the pot breaks the emulsion and this is the single commonest failure.
Pour the potash water in gradually while stirring. All at once and it will not disperse.
Sieve and discard the sediment. Undissolved potash is gritty and harsh.
The cue is unmistakable — the oil curdles and turns yellow. Keep going until all of it has, not most of it.
A pressure cooker for the cow foot. Two kilos of it on the stove is a very long afternoon.
Utazi is garnish only, sliced thin. It is bitter and a little goes a long way.
The wooden mortar is the serving vessel and it matters — it holds the heat and it is how nkwobi is recognised. Best served with chilled drinks: palm wine, beer or stout.
commonMistakes: Making the emulsion in a wet pot.
Adding the potash water in one go.
Under-cooking the cow foot, which should be yielding and gelatinous.
Treating utazi as a vegetable rather than a garnish.
sources: Adapted from 'Nkwobi', All Nigerian Recipes — no byline on the page, credited to the site. Quantities as printed: 2kg (4.4 lbs) cow foot, cut into sizeable pieces; 20cl (200ml) palm oil; 1 tablespoon powdered edible potash (Akanwu/Kaun/Keun); 1 teaspoon ground ehu; 2 big stock cubes; 1 medium onion; 2 habanero; salt to taste; utazi in thin slices and onion rings for garnish.

THE EMULSION CUE, verbatim: 'Pour the palm oil into a clean dry pot. Pour in the potash mixture (sieved) into the oil. Stir with a wooden spatula as you pour the potash. You'll notice the palm oil begin to curdle and turn yellow. Keep stirring till all the oil has turned yellow.' Note 'clean dry pot' — water in the pot breaks the emulsion, which is also why abacha is mixed off the stove.

NO COOKING TIME IS GIVEN on the page. The cow foot is cooked 'till well done' and the finished dish heated 'till the Nkwobi is piping hot'. A pressure cooker is recommended to save time. Yield is not formally given, though the page notes that '2 people that love Nkwobi can finish that in no time' for the 2 kg.

NKWOBI AGAINST ISI EWU, answered outright by this site on its isi ewu page: 'Nkwobi is prepared with cow foot while Isi Ewu…is prepared with goat head!' Setting the two ingredient lists side by side bears that out — same emulsion, same spice, same garnish, same vessel, same serving ritual. The differences are: cow foot against goat head; 200 ml palm oil against 150 ml; 1 teaspoon ground ehu against 2 teaspoons; crayfish in some nkwobi versions against doubled ehu in isi ewu; and utazi as a thin-sliced garnish in both, with isi ewu specifying about 10 leaves. Isi ewu also has a second emulsifier the nkwobi does not — the brain. See NGA060.
Serving, as printed on both pages: in a wooden mortar, garnished with utazi slices and onion rings, and 'Best served with chilled drinks: palm wine, beer or stout and soft drinks.'

For the alkali's chemistry, its functions and the safety note that belongs beside this recipe, see NGA120. In short: 'potash' is the wrong word — the mineral sold as kaun is trona, a sodium carbonate mineral, not potassium carbonate.
storage: 3 days refrigerated. The emulsion firms solid when cold.
reheating: Low heat, stirring, until the emulsion loosens and the meat is hot.
healthBenefits: Cow foot is exceptionally rich in collagen and gelatine.
Red palm oil provides carotenoids and vitamin E.
High in protein, iron and zinc.
culturalNote: Nkwobi is bar food, and the wooden mortar it arrives in is part of the performance — hot, glossy yellow, topped with onion rings and utazi, meant to be picked at slowly over a bottle. The same emulsion dresses goat head as isi ewu and shredded cassava as abacha, which makes the three of them a single family of bar dishes built on one piece of technique.
